{{Short description|Relation between vapour pressure and temperature}}
{{redirect2|Clapeyron equation|Clapeyron's equation|a state equation|ideal gas law}}

The '''Clausius–Clapeyron relation''', in [[chemical thermodynamics]], specifies the temperature dependence of pressure, most importantly [[vapor pressure]], at a discontinuous [[phase transition]] between two [[phases of matter]] of a single constituent. It is named after [[Rudolf Clausius]]<ref name="clausius">{{cite journal |last=Clausius |first=R. |year=1850 |title=Ueber die bewegende Kraft der Wärme und die Gesetze, welche sich daraus für die Wärmelehre selbst ableiten lassen |trans-title=On the motive power of heat and the laws which can be deduced therefrom regarding the theory of heat |url=http://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k15164w/f518.image |journal=Annalen der Physik |language=de |volume=155 |issue=4 |pages=500–524 |bibcode=1850AnP...155..500C |doi=10.1002/andp.18501550403 |hdl-access=free |hdl=2027/uc1.$b242250}}</ref> and [[Benoît Paul Émile Clapeyron]].<ref name="clapeyron">{{cite journal |last=Clapeyron |first=M. C. |year=1834 |title=Mémoire sur la puissance motrice de la chaleur |url=http://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k4336791/f157 |journal={{ill|Journal de l'École polytechnique|fr}} |language=fr |volume=23 |pages=153–190 |id=ark:/12148/bpt6k4336791/f157}}</ref> However, this relation was in fact originally derived by [[Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot|Sadi Carnot]] in his ''[[Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire]]'', which was published in 1824 but largely ignored until it was rediscovered by Clausius, Clapeyron, and [[Lord Kelvin]] decades later.<ref name="Feynman">{{cite web |url=https://www.feynmanlectures.caltech.edu/I_45.html |title=Illustrations of Thermodynamics |last=Feynman |first=Richard |author-link=Richard Feynman |date=1963 |website=The Feynman Lectures on Physics |publisher=California Institute of Technology |access-date=13 December 2023 |quote=This relationship was deduced by Carnot, but it is called the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.}}</ref> Kelvin said of Carnot's argument that "nothing in the whole range of Natural Philosophy is more remarkable than the establishment of general laws by such a process of reasoning."<ref name="Kelvin">{{cite journal |last=Thomson |first=William |date=1849 |title=An Account of Carnot's Theory of the Motive Power of Heat; with Numerical Results deduced from Regnault's Experiments on Steam |journal=Transactions of the Edinburgh Royal Society |volume=16 |issue=5 |pages=541–574 |doi=10.1017/S0080456800022481 |url=https://zenodo.org/record/2133961 |author-link=Lord Kelvin}}</ref>

Kelvin and his brother [[James Thomson (engineer)|James Thomson]] confirmed the relation experimentally in 1849–50, and it was historically important as a very early successful application of theoretical thermodynamics.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Pippard |first=Alfred B. |title=Elements of classical thermodynamics: for advanced students of physics |date=1981 |publisher=Univ. Pr |isbn=978-0-521-09101-5 |edition=Repr |location=Cambridge |page=116}}</ref> Its relevance to meteorology and [[climatology]] is the increase of the water-holding capacity of the atmosphere by about 7% for every 1&nbsp;°C (1.8&nbsp;°F) rise in temperature.

==Definition==
===Exact Clapeyron equation===
On a [[pressure]]–[[temperature]] (''P''–''T'') diagram, for any phase change the line separating the two phases is known as the [[Binodal|coexistence curve]]. The Clapeyron relation<ref>{{cite web |last1=Koziol |first1=Andrea |last2=Perkins |first2=Dexter |title=Teaching Phase Equilibria |url=https://serc.carleton.edu/research_education/equilibria/clapeyronequation.html |website=serc.carleton.edu |publisher=Carleton University |access-date=1 February 2023}}</ref><ref name="ChemLibreClausius">{{cite web | title=Clausius-Clapeyron Equation | website=Chemistry LibreTexts | date=2014-06-01 | url=https://chem.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry_Textbook_Maps/Supplemental_Modules_%28Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry%29/Physical_Properties_of_Matter/States_of_Matter/Phase_Transitions/Clausius-Clapeyron_Equation | access-date=2024-10-21}}</ref> gives the [[slope]] of the [[tangents]] to this curve. Mathematically,
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}T} = \frac{L}{T\,\Delta v} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta v},</math>
where <math>\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}T</math> is the slope of the tangent to the [[Binodal|coexistence curve]] at any point, <math>L</math> is the molar change in enthalpy ([[latent heat]], the amount of energy absorbed in the transformation), <math>T</math> is the [[temperature]], <math>\Delta v </math> is the [[molar volume]] change of the phase transition, and <math>\Delta s </math> is the [[molar entropy]] change of the phase transition. Alternatively, the specific values may be used instead of the molar ones.

===Clausius–Clapeyron equation===
The Clausius–Clapeyron equation<ref name="Wark1988">{{cite book |last=Wark |first=Kenneth |title=Thermodynamics |orig-date=1966 |edition=5th |year=1988 |publisher=McGraw-Hill, Inc. |location=New York, NY |isbn=978-0-07-068286-3 |chapter=Generalized Thermodynamic Relationships}}</ref>{{rp|p=509}} applies to vaporization of liquids where vapor follows [[ideal gas law]] using the [[Gas constant|ideal gas constant]] <math>R</math> and liquid volume is neglected as being much smaller than vapor volume ''V''. It is often used to calculate vapor pressure of a liquid.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Clausius-Clapeyron Equation |url=https://chemed.chem.purdue.edu/genchem/topicreview/bp/ch14/clausius.php |website=Bodner Research Web |publisher=Purdue University |access-date=1 February 2023}}</ref>

<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d} P}{\mathrm{d} T} = \frac {P L}{T^2 R},</math>

<math display="block">v = \frac{1}{n}= \frac{V}{N} = \frac{RT}{P}.</math>

where ''N'' is the [[amount of substance]] and ''n'' is the [[number density]].
The equation expresses this in a more convenient form just in terms of the latent heat, for moderate temperatures and pressures.

== Derivations ==
[[File:Phase-diag2.svg|thumb|300px|A typical [[phase diagram]]. The dotted green line gives the [[Properties of water#Density of water and ice|anomalous behavior of water]]. The Clausius–Clapeyron relation can be used to find the relationship between pressure and temperature along [[phase boundaries]].]]

=== Derivation from Gibbs–Duhem relation ===

Suppose two phases, <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math>, are in contact and at equilibrium with each other. Their chemical potentials are related by
<math display="block">\mu_\alpha = \mu_\beta.</math>

Furthermore, along the [[binodal|coexistence curve]],
<math display="block">\mathrm{d}\mu_\alpha = \mathrm{d}\mu_\beta.</math>

One may therefore use the [[Gibbs–Duhem]] relation
<math display="block">\mathrm{d}\mu = M(-s \, \mathrm{d}T + v \, \mathrm{d}P)</math>
(where <math>s</math> is the specific [[entropy]], <math>v</math> is the [[specific volume]], and <math>M</math> is the [[molar mass]]) to obtain
<math display="block">-(s_\beta - s_\alpha) \, \mathrm{d}T + (v_\beta - v_\alpha) \, \mathrm{d}P = 0.</math>

Rearrangement gives
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}T} = \frac{s_\beta - s_\alpha}{v_\beta - v_\alpha} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta v},</math>

from which the derivation of the Clapeyron equation continues as in [[#Derivation from state postulate|the previous section]].

===Ideal gas approximation at low temperatures===

When the [[phase transition]] of a substance is between a [[gas|gas phase]] and a condensed phase ([[liquid]] or [[solid]]), and occurs at temperatures much lower than the [[critical point (thermodynamics)|critical temperature]] of that substance, the [[specific volume]] of the gas phase <math>v_\text{g}</math> greatly exceeds that of the condensed phase <math>v_\text{c}</math>. Therefore, one may approximate
<math display="block">\Delta v = v_\text{g} \left(1 - \frac{v_\text{c}}{v_\text{g}}\right) \approx v_\text{g}</math>
at low [[temperatures]]. If [[pressure]] is also low, the gas may be approximated by the [[ideal gas law]], so that
<math display="block">v_\text{g} = \frac{RT}{P},</math>

where <math>P</math> is the pressure, <math>R</math> is the [[Gas constant#Specific gas constant|specific gas constant]], and <math>T</math> is the temperature. Substituting into the Clapeyron equation
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d} P}{\mathrm{d} T} = \frac{L}{T\,\Delta v},</math>
we can obtain the '''Clausius–Clapeyron equation'''<ref name="Wark1988"/>{{rp|p=509}}
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d} P}{\mathrm{d} T} = \frac {P L}{T^2 R}</math>
for low temperatures and pressures,<ref name="Wark1988"/>{{rp|p=509}} where <math>L</math> is the [[specific latent heat]] of the substance. Instead of the specific, corresponding molar values (i.e. <math>L</math> in kJ/mol and {{mvar|R}} = 8.31&nbsp;J/(mol⋅K)) may also be used.

Let <math>(P_1, T_1)</math> and <math>(P_2, T_2)</math> be any two points along the [[binodal|coexistence curve]] between two phases <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math>. In general, <math>L</math> varies between any two such points, as a function of temperature. But if <math>L</math> is approximated as constant,
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d} P}{P} \cong \frac {L}{R} \frac {\mathrm{d}T}{T^2},</math>
<math display="block">\int_{P_1}^{P_2} \frac{\mathrm{d}P}{P} \cong \frac{L}{R} \int_{T_1}^{T_2} \frac{\mathrm{d} T}{T^2},</math>
<math display="block">\ln P\Big|_{P=P_1}^{P_2} \cong -\frac{L}{R} \cdot \left.\frac{1}{T}\right|_{T=T_1}^{T_2},</math>
or<ref name="Cengel1998">{{cite book |last=Çengel |first=Yunus A. |author2=Boles, Michael A. |title=Thermodynamics – An Engineering Approach |orig-date=1989 |edition=3rd |series=McGraw-Hill Series in [[Mechanical Engineering]] |year=1998 |publisher=McGraw-Hill |location=Boston, MA. |isbn=978-0-07-011927-7}}</ref>{{rp|p=672}}<ref>{{cite book |last1=Masterton |first1=William L. |last2=Hurley |first2=Cecile N. |title=Chemistry: principles and reactions |date=2008 |publisher=Cengage Learning |isbn=978-0-495-12671-3 |page=230 |edition=6th |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=teubNK-b2bsC&q=clapeyron%20equation%20boiling |access-date=3 April 2020}}</ref>
<math display="block">\ln \frac{P_2}{P_1} \cong -\frac{L}{R} \left( \frac{1}{T_2} - \frac {1}{T_1} \right).</math>

These last equations are useful because they relate [[equilibrium vapor pressure|equilibrium]] or [[saturation vapor pressure]] and temperature to the latent heat of the phase change ''without'' requiring specific-volume data. For instance, for water near its [[normal boiling point]], with a molar enthalpy of vaporization of 40.7&nbsp;kJ/mol and {{mvar|R}} = 8.31&nbsp;J/(mol⋅K),
<math display="block">P_\text{vap}(T) \cong 1~\text{bar} \cdot \exp\left[-\frac{40\,700~\text{K}}{8.31} \left( \frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{373~\text{K}} \right) \right].</math>

===Clapeyron's derivation===
In the original work by Clapeyron, the following argument is advanced.<ref name="Clapeyrons argument">{{Cite journal |last=Clapeyron |first=E |date=1834 |title=Mémoire sur la puissance motrice de la chaleur  |journal= Journal de l ́École Polytechnique |volume=XIV  |pages=153–190}}</ref>
Clapeyron considered a Carnot process of saturated water vapor with horizontal isobars. As the pressure is a function of temperature alone, the isobars are also isotherms. If the process involves an infinitesimal amount of water, <math>\mathrm{d}x</math>, and an infinitesimal difference in temperature <math>\mathrm{d}T</math>, the heat absorbed is
<math display="block">Q = L\,\mathrm{d}x,</math>
and the corresponding work is
<math display="block">W = \frac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}T}\,\mathrm{d}T(V'' - V'),</math>
where <math>V'' - V'</math> is the difference between the volumes of <math>\mathrm{d}x</math> in the liquid phase and vapor phases.
The ratio <math>W/Q</math> is the efficiency of the Carnot engine, <math>\mathrm{d}T/T</math>.{{efn|In the original work, <math>1/T</math> was simply called the ''Carnot function'' and was not known in this form. Clausius determined the form 30 years later and added his name to the eponymous Clausius–Clapeyron relation.}} Substituting and rearranging gives
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}T} = \frac{L}{T(v'' - v')},</math>
where lowercase <math>v'' - v'</math> denotes the change in ''specific volume'' during the transition.

==Applications==

===Chemistry and chemical engineering===
For transitions between a gas and a condensed phase with the approximations described above, the expression may be rewritten as <ref name="ChemLibreClausius" />
<math display="block">\ln \left( \frac{P_1}{P_0} \right) = \frac{L}{R} \left( \frac{1}{T_0}-\frac{1}{T_1} \right) </math>
where <math>P_0, P_1</math> are the pressures at temperatures <math> T_0, T_1 </math> respectively and <math>R</math> is the [[Gas constant|ideal gas constant]]. For a liquid–gas transition, <math>L</math> is the [[molar latent heat]] (or [[molar enthalpy]]) of [[vaporization]]; for a solid–gas transition, <math>L</math> is the molar latent heat of [[Sublimation (chemistry)|sublimation]]. If the latent heat is known, then knowledge of one point on the [[binodal|coexistence curve]], for instance (1&nbsp;bar, 373&nbsp;K) for water, determines the rest of the curve. Conversely, the relationship between <math>\ln P</math> and <math>1/T</math> is linear, and so [[linear regression]] is used to estimate the latent heat.

===Meteorology and climatology===
[[Atmosphere|Atmospheric]] [[water vapor]] drives many important [[Meteorology|meteorologic]] phenomena (notably, [[precipitation]]), motivating interest in its [[Dynamical system|dynamics]]. The Clausius–Clapeyron equation for water vapor under typical atmospheric conditions (near [[standard temperature and pressure]]) is<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d} e_\text{s}}{\mathrm{d} T} = \frac{L_\text{v}(T) e_\text{s}}{R_\text{v} T^2},</math>where

{{unbulleted list | style = padding-left: 1em
| <math>e_\text{s}</math> is [[saturation vapor pressure]],| <math>T</math> is [[temperature]],| <math>L_\text{v}</math> is the [[specific latent heat]] of [[evaporation]] of water, and| <math>R_\text{v}</math> is the [[gas constant]] of water vapor.}}
The temperature dependence of the latent heat <math display="inline">L_\text{v}(T)</math> can be neglected in this application. The {{Anchor|August–Roche–Magnus formula|August–Roche–Magnus approximation}}'''[[Ernst Ferdinand August|August]]–[[Édouard Roche|Roche]]–[[Heinrich Gustav Magnus|Magnus]] formula''' provides a solution under that approximation:<ref>{{Citation
 |last1 = Alduchov |first1 = Oleg
 |last2 = Eskridge |first2 = Robert
 |date = 1997-11-01
 |title = Improved Magnus' Form Approximation of Saturation Vapor Pressure
 |url = http://www.osti.gov/scitech/servlets/purl/548871
 |publisher = [[NOAA]]
 | doi = 10.2172/548871
 |osti = 548871
 | doi-access = free
 }} Equation&nbsp;21 provides these coefficients.</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alduchov |first1=Oleg A. |last2=Eskridge |first2=Robert E. |title=Improved Magnus Form Approximation of Saturation Vapor Pressure |journal=Journal of Applied Meteorology |date=1996 |volume=35 |issue=4 |pages=601–609 |doi=10.1175/1520-0450(1996)035<0601:IMFAOS>2.0.CO;2 |bibcode=1996JApMe..35..601A |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc693874/ |doi-access=free}} Equation&nbsp;25 provides these coefficients.</ref>
<math display="block">e_\text{s}(T) = 6.1094 \exp \left( \frac{17.625 T}{T + 243.04} \right),</math>
where <math display="inline">e_\text{s}</math> is in [[Pascals|hPa]] and <math>T</math> is in [[degrees Celsius]] (whereas everywhere else on this page, <math>T</math> is an absolute temperature in units of kelvin).

The above formula is also sometimes called the ''Magnus'' or ''Magnus–Tetens'' approximation, though this attribution is historically inaccurate;<ref>{{cite journal |author1-link=Mark G. Lawrence |last1=Lawrence |first1=M. G. |title=The Relationship between Relative Humidity and the Dewpoint Temperature in Moist Air: A Simple Conversion and Applications |journal=Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society |date=2005 |volume=86 |issue=2 |pages=225–233 |doi=10.1175/BAMS-86-2-225 |url=http://climate.envsci.rutgers.edu/pdf/LawrenceRHdewpointBAMS.pdf |bibcode=2005BAMS...86..225L}}</ref> see also the [[Vapour pressure of water#Accuracy of different formulations|discussion of the accuracy of different approximating formulae for saturation vapour pressure of water]].

Under typical atmospheric conditions, the [[denominator]] in the [[exponent]] <math display="inline">T + 243.04</math> depends weakly on <math display="inline">T</math>. Therefore, the August–Roche–Magnus formula implies that saturation vapor pressure changes approximately [[exponential function|exponentially]] with temperature under typical atmospheric conditions, and hence the water-holding capacity of the atmosphere increases by about 7% for every 1&nbsp;°C rise in temperature.<ref>IPCC, Climate Change 2007: Working Group I: The Physical Science Basis, [http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg1/en/faq-3-2.html "FAQ 3.2 How is Precipitation Changing?"]. {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181102212322/http://www.ipcc.ch/publications_and_data/ar4/wg1/en/faq-3-2.html |date=2018-11-02 }}.</ref>

== Example ==
One of the uses of this equation is to determine if a phase transition will occur in a given situation. Consider the question of how much pressure is needed to melt ice at a temperature <math>{\Delta T}</math> below 0&nbsp;°C. Note that water is unusual in that its change in volume upon melting is negative. We can assume
<math display="block">\Delta P = \frac{L}{T\,\Delta v} \, \Delta T,</math>
and substituting in
{{unbulleted list | style = padding-left: 1.6em
| <math>L = 3.34 \times 10^5~\mathrm{J/kg}</math> (latent heat of fusion for water),
| <math>T = 273 \, \mathrm{K}</math> (absolute temperature in [[kelvin]]s),
| <math>\Delta v = -9.05 \times 10^{-5}~\mathrm{m^3 / kg}</math> (change in specific volume from solid to liquid),
}}
we obtain
<math display="block">\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta T} = -13.5~\text{MPa}/\text{K}.</math>

To provide a rough example of how much pressure this is, to melt ice at −7&nbsp;°C (the temperature many [[ice skating]] rinks are set at) would require balancing a small car on an area around 1cm<sup>2</sup>. This shows that ice skating cannot be simply explained by pressure-caused melting point depression, and in fact the mechanism is quite complex.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Liefferink |first1=Rinse W. |last2=Hsia |first2=Feng-Chun |last3=Weber |first3=Bart |last4=Bonn |first4=Daniel |date=2021-02-08 |title=Friction on Ice: How Temperature, Pressure, and Speed Control the Slipperiness of Ice |journal=Physical Review X |volume=11 |issue=1 |article-number=011025 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevX.11.011025|doi-access=free |hdl=11245.1/a901a712-0a68-42ca-a80f-732e541288d2 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== Second derivative ==
While the Clausius–Clapeyron relation gives the slope of the coexistence curve, it does not provide any information about its curvature or [[second derivative]]. The second derivative of the coexistence curve of phases 1 and 2 is given by<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Krafcik | first1 = Matthew
 | last2 = Sánchez Velasco | first2 = Eduardo
 | title = Beyond Clausius–Clapeyron: Determining the second derivative of a first-order phase transition line
 | journal = American Journal of Physics
 | volume = 82
 | issue = 4
 | pages = 301–305
 | date = 2014
 | doi = 10.1119/1.4858403|bibcode = 2014AmJPh..82..301K }}</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
 \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 P}{\mathrm{d} T^2} &= \frac{1}{v_2 - v_1} \left[\frac{c_{p2} - c_{p1}}{T} - 2(v_2\alpha_2 - v_1\alpha_1) \frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}T}\right] \\
 {} &+ \frac{1}{v_2 - v_1}\left[(v_2 \kappa_{T2} - v_1 \kappa_{T1}) \left(\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}T}\right)^2\right],
\end{align}
</math>
where subscripts 1 and 2 denote the different phases, <math>c_p</math> is the [[specific heat capacity]] at constant pressure, <math>\alpha = (1/v)(\mathrm{d}v/\mathrm{d}T)_P</math> is the [[thermal expansion coefficient]], and <math>\kappa_T = -(1/v)(\mathrm{d}v/\mathrm{d}P)_T</math> is the [[isothermal compressibility]].
